title: Interpreting Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks
claim: A black-box policy is distilled into a surrogate where a learned router mixes interpretable programs, trained by combined textual and numerical gradients.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right flow, nested surrogate box, legend below, dashed backward arrows
description: A single block diagram with a wide hatched 'Black Box NCO Model' bar across the top. It receives 'state' and outputs 'teacher action' on the right. Below it, a light-blue rounded box labeled 'surrogate' holds the student pathway. State feeds a hatched 'Router', which outputs weights ω1, ω2 and ω3. Each weight goes to one of three purple code-file icons labeled 'programs'. The state also feeds these programs as 'program input'. The program outputs combine at a Σ node and produce 'student action'. A blue double-headed arrow marked ℒ links teacher and student actions. Dashed blue backward arrows carry numerical gradients (▽) to the router. TextGrad, shown with an AI atom icon, sends LLM revisions to the programs. A boxed legend at the bottom explains the symbols: neural vs interpretable fills, forward vs backward arrows, LLM revise/edit, and numerical gradient.
caption: Framework of Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB).
abstract: While Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) achieves strong performance, its interpretability remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB), the first post-hoc, surrogate-based interpretability method for NCO, which explains a black-box policy by distilling it into an interpretable behavior surrogate. A natural surrogate is a Concept Bottleneck Model (CBM), yet standard concepts are input attributes, whereas NCO is better explained by decision rules that are hard to predefine. EPB thus uses LLMs to evolve a bank of programmatic decision rules as concepts, each producing an action distribution, where a learned state-dependent router then mixes them to form the surrogate action. We optimize EPB through an iterative framework: Block I fixes the bank size and introduces the hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent to jointly optimize the textual programs and the numerical router; Block II adapts the bank size via failure-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the EPB surrogate closely matches the teacher's behavior and solution quality. We then analyze the distilled rules, reveal several NCO decision patterns, and verify the rules' faithfulness to the surrogate's decisions. Moreover, the surrogate allows targeted program edits that improve its generalization beyond the teacher. Our work advances interpretable NCO and establishes EPB as a promising direction for interpreting complex learned decision-making policies.
